standard.title: Managed food and fibre production
standard.description: Explain how and why food and fibre are produced in managed environments
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe the ways of producing food and fibre (AC9TDE4K03). They understand that food and fibre come from different production systems. They have not yet explained how and why those environments are actively managed — the decisions, constraints, and sustainability practices behind production.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how food and fibre are produced in managed environments, including soil preparation, plant and animal selection, and supply chain processes, and why these management decisions are made.

nodes.label: Why food and fibre production requires active management
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why food and fibre production requires deliberate management decisions rather than just natural growth
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two management decisions made in a food or fibre production environment and explain why each decision is made
nodes.typical_width: Explain how soil preparation, plant selection and animal breed selection are management decisions made to match the environment; describe why specific plants or animals suit specific climates or regions — connecting environmental conditions to production outcomes
wider: Investigate how before colonisation, First Nations Australians managed food and fibre resources sustainably — including the cultivation of bunya nuts, macadamia and finger limes — and how some of these are now commercially cultivated to meet domestic and international demand

Compare tropical food production (northern Australia — higher temperature, tropical fruits) with temperate food production (cooler regions — sheep, cool-climate crops) — explaining how environment shapes management choices
Investigate and experiment with soil preparation methods (composting, mulching, nutrient cycling) and explain how each improves soil quality and production sustainability

response_modes.reason: Students tend to think of food production as natural rather than designed. Multiple managed environment contexts — different climates, different species, different management decisions — help students see production as a system of deliberate choices responsive to environmental constraints.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations pre-colonial resource management context is genuinely rich — it presents sustainable food and fibre management as a long-standing designed system, not just a contemporary environmental aspiration, and creates direct comparison with modern commercial practices.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two management decisions in food or fibre production
Explains why each decision is made — connecting it to a production goal or environmental constraint
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain why management decisions are made cannot sequence supply chain stages meaningfully in N2 — the 'why' of each stage (soil prep timing, harvest scheduling) requires understanding the management rationale, not just the step order.

nodes.label: Supply chains — from production to retail
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can sequence and explain the process of converting on-farm food or fibre products into a product suitable for retail sale
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three stages in a paddock-to-plate or fibre-to-garment supply chain and explain what happens at each stage
nodes.typical_width: Sequence the full supply chain for a food or fibre product — from production through processing to retail; explain what value is added at each stage and why each step is necessary; represent the chain visually (e.g. flowchart, diagram)
wider: Create a digital flowchart representing a paddock-to-plate supply chain for a locally grown product — annotating each stage with the management decisions and technologies involved
Sequence the fibre-to-garment life cycle (fibre → yarn → fabric → garment) and explain how decisions at each stage affect the sustainability and quality of the final product
Visit or virtually tour a farm and investigate how on-site decisions (breed selection, soil management, harvesting timing) affect the quality and quantity of product reaching the consumer

response_modes.reason: Students commonly know the end product and the raw material but cannot sequence the transformation steps. Tracing the supply chain as a connected sequence — where the output of each stage is the input of the next — makes the managed system legible as a designed process.

success_criteria: Sequences at least three stages in a food or fibre supply chain in correct order
Explains what happens at each stage
